summary: Defines BGP Link State extensions for advertising Flexible Algorithm definitions and related information. This lets a controller or other BGP-LS consumer learn about flexible algorithms that routers are running in OSPF and IS-IS.

eli5.summary: Routers have special routing rules in their own club. This lets an outside helper learn those rules by listening in through a shared messenger.

questions: how to advertise flex-algo definitions in bgp-ls
bgp link state extensions for segment routing
what is a flexible algorithm definition tlv
subtitle: New BGP-LS TLVs that let controllers learn how routers define their Flexible Algorithms.

tldr.problem: Flexible Algorithm lets OSPF and IS-IS compute paths using user-defined metrics and constraints, but the algorithm definitions live inside the IGP. Anything outside the IGP, such as a controller using BGP-LS, could not learn them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a Flexible Algorithm Definition TLV with six sub-TLVs for the Node NLRI, and a Flexible Algorithm Prefix Metric TLV for the Prefix NLRI, each derived from the matching IGP advertisement in RFC 9350.
tldr.outcome: BGP-LS consumers can map a Flexible Algorithm number to its definition in each IGP area or domain, which helps set up end-to-end SR Policy paths across domains.

today: RFC 9351 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2023. It is not obsoleted or updated by another RFC, and it builds on the IGP Flexible Algorithm specification in RFC 9350.

sections.title: Why BGP-LS Needs Flex-Algo Data
sections.content:
Classical IGP (OSPF and IS-IS) path computation is based on the IGP metric on links. Many networks use RSVP-TE (RFC 3209) or Segment Routing (SR) Policy (RFC 8402) to push traffic over paths computed with other metrics or constraints. RFC 9350 defines Flexible Algorithm, which lets the IGPs themselves compute constraint-based paths.

Flexible Algorithm lets a user choose the type of calculation (such as shortest path), the metric type (such as IGP metric or TE metric) and the constraints (such as including or excluding links by affinity).

BGP-LS already carries some SR information, including the SR Algorithm TLV, the Prefix-SID TLV and the SRv6 Locator TLV (defined in RFC 9085 for SR-MPLS and in an Internet-Draft for SRv6). What was missing is the Flexible Algorithm Definition (FAD) itself. This document adds it so a consumer can learn the mapping from algorithm number to definition in each area or domain.

With that, an SR Policy (RFC 9256) can be built end to end across domains. For example, choosing the Flex-Algo Prefix-SID or End SID of border routers for a delay-optimizing definition builds a low-latency path across IGP domains with few SIDs in the list.
sections.eli5: Routers in each neighborhood agree on special travel rules, like 'fastest road only'. This RFC gives an outside planner a way to read those rules so it can plan trips across neighborhoods.

sections.title: Where the New TLVs Attach
sections.content:
BGP-LS (RFC 7752) has Node, Link and Prefix NLRI, each with a BGP-LS Attribute. This document adds data to two of them. The FADs a node advertises are a node-level attribute and go with the Node NLRI. The Flexible Algorithm Prefix Metric (FAPM) is a prefix attribute and goes with the Prefix NLRI.

Link attributes used in Flex-Algo calculation, such as affinities and Shared Risk Link Groups (SRLG), are already advertised in the IGPs using Application-Specific Link Attribute (ASLA) advertisements. Their BGP-LS extensions are in RFC 9294, so this document does not repeat them.

All the new TLVs are optional and derived from the matching IS-IS or OSPF advertisements in RFC 9350.
sections.eli5: The rules about a whole router go on the router's card, and the extra cost for reaching a place goes on that place's card.

sections.title: The Flexible Algorithm Definition TLV
sections.content:
The FAD TLV (type 1039) is an optional BGP-LS Attribute TLV on the Node NLRI. Its length covers the value field including sub-TLVs and MUST be 4 or larger. After Type and Length come four single-octet fields: the Flex Algo number (between 128 and 255 inclusive), Metric-Type, Calc-Type and Priority, all as defined in RFC 9350. Zero or more sub-TLVs follow.

In IS-IS it is derived from the Flexible Algorithm Definition sub-TLV, and in OSPFv2 or OSPFv3 from the OSPF Flexible Algorithm Definition TLV. A node's attribute may hold several FAD TLVs, one per algorithm it advertises.

Six sub-TLVs are defined:

  • Exclude-Any Affinity (1040): exclude links with any listed affinity.
  • Include-Any Affinity (1041): include links with any listed affinity.
  • Include-All Affinity (1042): include links with all listed affinities.
  • Definition Flags (1043): a bitmask of FAD flags.
  • Exclude SRLG (1045): exclude links in any listed SRLG.
  • Unsupported (1046): lists sub-TLV types the originating node does not understand.

The three affinity sub-TLVs use the Extended Admin Group (RFC 7308) encoding. Their lengths, and those of Flags and SRLG, MUST be non-zero and a multiple of 4. SRLG values are 4 octets each.
sections.eli5: The main card says which rule set this is. Extra stickers say which roads to avoid, which roads are required, and a warning sticker if the sender could not read some of the rules.

sections.title: The Unsupported Sub-TLV
sections.content:
FAD is different from most extensions, where skipping an unknown sub-TLV is harmless. RFC 9350 says everyone using a FAD for computation must understand all of it. If the BGP-LS node cannot handle some sub-TLV in the IGP advertisement, it would otherwise pass on an incomplete definition.

The Flexible Algorithm Unsupported sub-TLV carries a Protocol-ID (the BGP-LS protocol the FAD came from) followed by the sub-TLV types that are not supported. A type is 1 octet for IS-IS and 2 octets for OSPF.

The originating node MUST include this sub-TLV when it meets an unsupported sub-TLV in the IGP FAD, and SHOULD list the unsupported types as a diagnostic aid. It is RECOMMENDED to originate IGP topology into BGP-LS from a node that supports all FAD extensions in use in its part of the network, to avoid an incomplete FAD being advertised. How consumers use FAD information is out of scope.
sections.eli5: If the messenger cannot read part of a rule, it must say so on the note, so nobody thinks they have the whole rulebook when they do not.

sections.title: Prefix Metric TLV and Code Points
sections.content:
The Flexible Algorithm Prefix Metric TLV (FAPM, type 1044) attaches to the Prefix NLRI and has length 8 octets. Its fields are the Flex Algo number (128 to 255), Flags (single octet, only for OSPF, MUST be 0 for IS-IS), a 2-octet Reserved field (set to 0 by the sender, ignored by the receiver) and a 4-octet Metric. It comes from the IS-IS or OSPF Flexible Algorithm Prefix Metric sub-TLV in RFC 9350, and a prefix may carry one per algorithm.

IANA allocated code points 1039 through 1046 in the BGP-LS Node Descriptor, Link Descriptor, Prefix Descriptor, and Attribute TLVs registry, as the table in the viz lists.
sections.eli5: Each place can have its own extra cost for each rule set, written as a number on its card.

sections.title: Manageability and Security
sections.content:
The extensions add to the IGP topology information already distributed through RFC 7752 and do not change BGP operation. The malformed-attribute tests in the Fault Management section of RFC 7752 now cover the new TLVs. No new configuration or monitoring is defined.

For security, RFC 7752 covers acquiring and distributing BGP-LS information, and the IGP instances originating the data are assumed to provide the security RFC 9350 requires. Tampering with Flex-Algo information could affect applications using it, including route calculation and programming, but because the data relates to a specific Flex-Algo topology, the impact is similarly limited in scope.
sections.eli5: Messing with these notes could confuse the planner, but only for the one rule set the notes belong to.
